prompt: In a PET scan, each positron emitted by the tracer quickly meets an electron. What does the scanner detect?
choices: two gamma rays traveling in opposite directions
two alpha particles traveling in opposite directions
a single beta particle from the tracer
neutrons released from the tracer nucleus
answer: two gamma rays traveling in opposite directions
hint: A positron is the antimatter partner of an electron. When matter and antimatter meet, their mass becomes energy.
explain: The positron and electron annihilate, and their mass turns into two gamma rays (511 keV each) that fly off in opposite directions. Detectors around the patient pick up each pair, which locates the tracer in the body.

prompt: Iodine-131 is a beta emitter used to treat an overactive thyroid gland. Why does it destroy thyroid tissue while causing little damage to the rest of the body?
choices: Iodine collects in the thyroid, and beta particles have a short range.
Beta particles pass through other tissues without being absorbed.
I-131 emits alpha particles that can travel only to the thyroid.
I-131 becomes radioactive only after the thyroid absorbs it.
answer: Iodine collects in the thyroid, and beta particles have a short range.
hint: Where in the body does iodine collect? How far do beta particles travel in tissue?
explain: The thyroid takes up iodide to make its hormones, so I-131 collects there. Its beta particles travel only a few millimeters in tissue, so the dose is delivered mainly to the thyroid. Radioactive decay does not depend on location in the body.
